report.incidentSummary: On 2026-09-14 at 09:15 IST (03:45 UTC, market open), approximately 15.6% of stock orders placed through order-service failed with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable errors. The trading desk reported failures affecting about one in five orders and suspected the database due to a concurrent database CPU rise to ~77%. Investigation showed the database was healthy, with no connection pool exhaustion or query timeouts. Instead, the incident was caused by the external broker API (broker-api) enforcing a strict rate limit of 300 requests/second. Market-open order submission reached over 750 orders/sec (45,252 orders/min), driving broker-connector request rates to 1,055 req/s. The broker responded with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, exhausting order-service retries. The incident auto-mitigated at 04:21 UTC (09:51 IST) once order volume subsided below 300 req/s.
report.rootCauseStatement: The stock order failures at market open were caused by external broker API rate limiting (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests). At the 09:15 IST open, incoming stock orders spiked to 45,252 orders/minute (>750 orders/sec), driving outbound order traffic through broker-connector to a peak of 1,055 req/s. The broker API strictly enforces an order rate limit of 300 req/s and rejected excess orders with HTTP 429. Because broker-connector lacks client-side rate limiting or request smoothing, order-service exhausted its retry budget and returned HTTP 503 to end users. The concurrent database CPU spike was benign market-open portfolio viewing activity and did not cause connection starvation or order errors.

hypotheses.cause: External broker API (broker-api) strictly enforced a 300 req/s order rate limit. Market-open order volume (>750 orders/sec incoming, peaking at 1,055 req/s to broker-connector) exceeded this threshold, causing broker-api to return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and order-service to reject orders with HTTP 503 after retries.
hypotheses.rationale: Directly supported by broker-connector HTTP 429 logs and rate_limited_count metrics, order-service HTTP 503 retry-exhaustion logs, and the exact timing alignment: failures started when request_rate exceeded 300 req/s and vanished the minute request_rate fell below 300 req/s.

hypotheses.cause: Primary database CPU spike caused database query timeouts and connection pool starvation for order-service, leading to rejected orders.
hypotheses.rationale: Ruled out: order-service connection pool in use peaked at 42.84/100, db_pool_wait_ms was negligible (max 5.14 ms), lock wait times were flat (~4 ms), and order-service logged no database connection/query errors, only broker rate limit (429) errors.

hypotheses.cause: order-service CPU saturation or host resource exhaustion caused order processing failures at market open.
hypotheses.rationale: Ruled out: order-service CPU peaked at 64.71%, well below saturation, and logged errors were explicitly due to broker rate limiting.

facts.statement: At 03:45 UTC (09:15 IST market open), orders_per_min on order-service surged from ~4,700/min to 45,252/min, and order-service error_rate jumped from ~0.4% baseline to 15.61% at 03:46 UTC, persisting around 15.4%-15.6% until 04:17 UTC.
order-service logged 281 HTTP 503 errors between 03:45 UTC and 04:20 UTC with the message 'order <ref> rejected: broker rate limit (429) after 2 retries'.
broker-connector logged 378 HTTP 429 errors from provider broker-api on POST /orders stating '429 Too Many Requests (limit 300 req/s; retry-after 1s)'.

broker-connector request_rate spiked to 1,055 req/s at 03:45 UTC and remained over 300 req/s until 04:20 UTC. During this window, rate_limited_count reached up to 809.5/min and broker-connector error_rate stayed at ~11.3%. At 04:21 UTC, when request_rate dropped to ~303 req/s, rate_limited_count dropped to 0 and error_rate fell to 0.20%.

Database CPU utilization increased from ~37% to 76.87% at 03:45 UTC, but active_connections remained steady at ~175, query rate stayed at ~4,000 qps, db_lock_wait_ms remained normal (~4 ms), and order-service db_pool_in_use peaked at 42.84 out of 100 max connections with db_pool_wait_ms at only 2.2-5.1 ms.

The slow queries observed on the database during the window were 'SELECT ... FROM holdings WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY updated_at' from portfolio-service due to market-open user traffic (portfolio-service request rate rose from ~850 to 1,655 req/s), while portfolio-service error rate stayed flat at ~0.2%.

inferences.statement: Outbound request rate on broker-connector (peak 1,055 req/s) was higher than the incoming order rate (~754 orders/s) because failed order attempts triggered rapid retries, amplifying traffic against broker-api.

The database CPU spike to ~77% was normal market-open load caused by thousands of users opening the app to view their portfolios, generating holdings queries on portfolio-service, and was completely independent of the order failure mechanism.

assumptions.statement: Market open order volumes are anticipated to routinely peak above 300 orders/sec on high-volatility trading days unless rate-controlled or negotiated with the broker.

timeline.event: Normal pre-market trading baseline: order-service processing ~2,000-5,000 orders/min with error rate ~0.4%; broker-connector request rate ~100-130 req/s.
Market opens (09:15 IST). User order submissions surge to 45,252 orders/min on order-service. Outbound requests from broker-connector to broker-api surge to 1,055 req/s. Database CPU rises to 50.4%.
broker-api begins rejecting order requests exceeding 300 req/s with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. broker-connector logs first 429 errors.
order-service logs HTTP 503 rejections after retrying 429 responses. Error rate on order-service jumps to 15.61%. Database CPU reaches ~73-76% with slow portfolio holdings queries.
Trading desk reports INC-4849: about one in five stock orders failing, noting database CPU spike.
Market open order surge subsides. broker-connector request rate drops below 300 req/s (299.3 req/s at 04:18, 292.9 req/s at 04:20).
broker-connector rate_limited_count drops to 0. order-service error rate returns to normal baseline (0.29%). Incident fully auto-mitigated.

confidence.rationale: Comprehensive metric and log evidence across order-service, broker-connector, database, and api-gateway confirms that order-service rejected orders with HTTP 503 due to upstream HTTP 429 rate limit errors from broker-api. Database metrics conclusively rule out database pool exhaustion, lock contention, or CPU bottleneck as the cause of order failures.

gaps.description: Broker-connector log query returned sampled logs (e.g., sampled 1/50 or 1/100) rather than full unsampled logs of every 429 response.
gaps.impact: No impact on root cause identification; exact error counts are accurately reflected by the rate_limited_count and error_rate metrics.

recommendedActions.action: Implement client-side rate limiting and an order queuing/smoothing buffer in broker-connector (e.g., token bucket capped at 300 req/s) so orders exceeding the burst limit are queued and paced rather than immediately rejected with 429.
recommendedActions.rationale: broker-api enforces a strict 300 req/s quota. Without client-side rate limiting or pacing, any traffic spike above 300 req/s immediately causes 429s and user-facing order drops.
recommendedActions.verification: Simulate market-open bursts (>500 req/s) in staging; verify broker-connector paces outbound requests to broker-api at <=300 req/s and buffers excess requests without triggering 429 responses.

recommendedActions.action: Configure exponential backoff with jitter on order-service retries for broker 429 responses, respecting the 'Retry-After' header sent by broker-api.
recommendedActions.rationale: Currently order-service retries up to 2-3 times without sufficient backoff, exacerbating the rate-limit storm against broker-api.
recommendedActions.verification: Verify in test environment that when broker-api returns 429 with Retry-After: 1s, order-service pauses retries accordingly instead of immediately resending.

recommendedActions.action: Engage partner broker to request an increase in order API rate limits above 300 req/s to accommodate growing platform market-open order volume.
recommendedActions.rationale: Platform peak volume at market open (45,252 orders/min = 754 orders/sec) inherently exceeds the current contractual rate limit of 300 req/s.
recommendedActions.verification: Check broker API quota documentation and broker agreement confirmation for increased per-second order rate limit.

recommendedActions.action: Update the market-open runbook to decouple database CPU dashboard observations from trading order failures unless connection pool wait times (db_pool_wait_ms) or lock wait metrics actually elevate.
recommendedActions.rationale: Database CPU spikes at market open are expected due to user logins and portfolio queries, which led on-call to falsely suspect the database.
recommendedActions.verification: Review runbook with trading and database on-call teams during incident retrospective.

# Investigation report: Orders erroring at the open

**Outcome:** conclusive · **Stop reason:** completed · **Confidence:** 0.95 · **Written by:** baseline agent

## Summary
On 2026-09-14 at 09:15 IST (03:45 UTC, market open), approximately 15.6% of stock orders placed through order-service failed with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable errors. The trading desk reported failures affecting about one in five orders and suspected the database due to a concurrent database CPU rise to ~77%. Instead, the incident was caused by the external broker API (broker-api) enforcing a strict rate limit of 300 requests/second. Market-open order submission reached over 750 orders/sec (45,252 orders/min), driving broker-connector request rates to 1,055 req/s. The broker responded with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, exhausting order-service retries. The incident auto-mitigated at 04:21 UTC (09:51 IST) once order volume subsided below 300 req/s.

**Root cause:** The stock order failures at market open were caused by external broker API rate limiting (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests). At the 09:15 IST open, incoming stock orders spiked to 45,252 orders/minute (>750 orders/sec), driving outbound order traffic through broker-connector to a peak of 1,055 req/s. The broker API strictly enforces an order rate limit of 300 req/s and rejected excess orders with HTTP 429. Because broker-connector lacks client-side rate limiting or request smoothing, order-service exhausted its retry budget and returned HTTP 503 to end users. The concurrent database CPU spike was benign market-open portfolio viewing activity and did not cause connection starvation or order errors.

## Hypotheses

- Outbound request rate on broker-connector (peak 1,055 req/s) was higher than the incoming order rate (~754 orders/s) because failed order attempts triggered rapid retries, amplifying traffic against broker-api. [ev_5, ev_12]
- The database CPU spike to ~77% was normal market-open load caused by thousands of users opening the app to view their portfolios, generating holdings queries on portfolio-service, and was completely independent of the order failure mechanism. [ev_1, ev_6, ev_7, ev_19]
